What a sandfly is, and why it matters

blocks.x: Sandflies are tiny, hairy, night-biting flies. They matter for one reason above all: they are the only vectors of Leishmania. Learn the fly and you have already learned half of leishmaniasis.

items: Class: Insecta · Order: Diptera
Sub-order: Nematocera · Family: Psychodidae
Subfamily: Phlebotominae — this is the name to remember; "phlebotomine sandfly" means a blood-feeding sandfly.

blocks.x: There are about 700 species of phlebotomine sandflies, but only about 90 are anthropophagous (willing to bite humans). Most sandflies are therefore of no medical importance at all.
The six genera — split by hemisphere
This split is heavily examined, and it is easy if you anchor it on the two <term d="An organism that transmits a pathogen from one host to another.">vector</term> genera:

items: Old World: Phlebotomus, Sergentomyia, Chinius
New World: Lutzomyia, Brumptomyia, Warileya

blocks.x: Phlebotomus = Old World, Lutzomyia = New World. Every leishmaniasis question about "which vector" comes back to that one line.
What sandflies transmit

items: Leishmaniasis — the big one
Sandfly fever
Carrion's disease
Vesicular stomatitis virus

blocks.x: Three features identify a sandfly on sight: it is tiny, it is hairy, and its wings are held up in a V even while it feeds.

items: Size: 1.5–3.5 mm — among the smallest biting flies.
Appearance: distinctly hairy, with large black eyes and long legs.
Mouthparts: piercing, for taking blood.
Wings: hairy, and held erect at about a 40° angle over the body at rest and during blood feeding. Most flies fold their wings flat — a sandfly does not.
Movement: a characteristic hopping/jumping flight rather than sustained flying.

blocks.x: Note: identifying phlebotomine sandflies to species level is difficult, which is why control programmes usually work at genus level.

sections.title: Four stages, and none of them in water

blocks.x: The sandfly is holometabolous — egg, larva, pupa, adult. The single most important exam point: sandfly eggs need humidity but are not laid in water. This is what separates them from mosquitoes.

items: Eggs hatch after 4–20 days.
Larvae pass through four instars, completed in 20–30 days. They are scavengers, feeding on decaying organic matter.
Larval diapause (a pause in development) can occur, driven by temperature and nutrient availability.
Pupal stage lasts 6–13 days before the adult emerges.

blocks.x: As with mosquitoes, only the female takes blood, and for the same reason — she needs it to make eggs.

items: Both sexes feed on plant juices and sugary secretions for energy.
Females additionally feed on blood to produce eggs.
They are pool feeders: the mouthparts probe and lacerate the skin, creating a small pool of blood which the fly then drinks. They do not cannulate a vessel.
Feeding is influenced by temperature, humidity and air movement.
Most species bite at dusk and during the night, when temperature falls and humidity rises.
Most feed outdoors, though daytime biting happens indoors in darkened rooms, or among shaded vegetation if the flies are disturbed.

blocks.x: Reproduction and egg laying

items: Adults mate soon after emergence; males find females at resting sites or on the host, helped by pheromones.
A female lays 30–70 eggs per gonotrophic cycle.
Eggs are deposited in cracks and holes in the ground or buildings, animal burrows and among tree roots.
Eggs need a high-humidity microhabitat to survive, but are not laid in water.
Generally one blood meal produces one batch of eggs.

sections.title: Where they live and what they bite

items: Phlebotomus species occur mainly in warm, humid, tropical climates, typically in savannah and semi-desert vegetation; a few reach temperate zones.
They colonise rural, peri-urban and urban areas alike.
Larvae need a cool, moist habitat with decaying debris.
Adults rest in rock crevices, caves and rodent burrows, and around houses in cool, dark, humid corners of animal shelters and dwellings.
Rodent burrows and peridomestic areas are favoured because they provide both shelter and a ready blood supply.

blocks.x: <term d="The tendency of a vector to feed on particular host species.">Host preference</term>

items: Females feed on a wide range of vertebrates: humans, livestock, dogs, urban and wild rodents, reptiles, amphibians and birds.
Each species has its own preferences, but host availability is a major determinant.
Where many animals are present, Phlebotomus perfiliewi and P. perniciosus were found to feed on all of them — showing host choice is driven by what is around.
In urban and peri-urban settings, humans and domestic dogs are the main targets — and the dog is also the reservoir, which is why urban leishmaniasis persists.

sections.title: Controlling sandflies — and why the larvae are the hard part

blocks.x: The central difficulty: the breeding sites of most species are unknown, so larval control is largely impossible. Control therefore targets the adult, the host and the reservoir.

items: Insecticides — against resting adults.
Personal protection — repellents, protective clothing, fine-mesh nets (ordinary bednet mesh can be too coarse for so small a fly).
Habitat reduction/modification.
Destroying the habitat of reservoir hosts, and reservoir control (notably dogs and rodents).
Biological control: Bacillus sphaericus reduces survival and fecundity of phlebotomine sandflies.

blocks.x: Leishmania are intracellular parasites of blood and tissues. The whole disease turns on one fact: the parasite lives inside macrophages — the very cells meant to destroy it.
Two forms, two hosts — learn this pair first

items: Amastigote — the form in humans and other vertebrates. No free flagellum, round, lives inside macrophages.
Promastigote — the form in the intestine of the sandfly. Flagellated, motile, and the infective stage.

blocks.x: Memory hook: amastigote = absent flagellum = in a human. Promastigote is the one that propels itself, in the fly.
Burden

items: A zoonotic infection affecting about 12 million people in 88 countries.
Local data: 3–4% reported cases and 12–32% suspected cases in the Ho municipality (Kweku et al., 2011).

blocks.x: The four species of medical importance

items: Leishmania tropica
Leishmania braziliensis
Leishmania mexicana
Leishmania donovani

blocks.x: All are transmitted by sandflies of the genus Phlebotomus (Old World) or Lutzomyia (New World).
Amastigote morphology

items: Small, round to oval bodies, 2–4 µm depending on species.
Seen in groups inside macrophages, or lying free between cells.
Nucleus and kinetoplast stain dark reddish-mauve; the cytoplasm stains palely.
Crucially, amastigote morphology is identical for all Leishmania species — so you cannot tell the species down the microscope. That is exactly why culture, PCR and clinical picture matter.

sections.title: One life cycle for all four species

blocks.x: All four species share the same life cycle; only the tissue they end up in differs. Follow it as a loop with two halves — what happens in the human, and what happens in the fly.
In the human

items: An infected sandfly bites and injects promastigotes (the infective stage, carried in its saliva) into the skin.
The promastigotes lose their flagella and become amastigotes.
Amastigotes are taken up by macrophages and other reticuloendothelial cells — and survive inside them.
They multiply until the cell ruptures, releasing parasites to infect more cells.
In visceral disease this destroys organs such as the liver and spleen.

blocks.x: In the sandfly

items: A sandfly bites an infected person and picks up amastigotes.
These transform into promastigotes, which multiply by binary fission in the midgut.
They then migrate to the proboscis, ready to be injected into the next person.

blocks.x: There are three clinical forms — cutaneous (skin), mucocutaneous (skin plus mucous membranes) and visceral (internal organs). Tie each to its species, its vector and its world.
Leishmania tropica — <term d="Skin-limited leishmaniasis producing an ulcer that heals with scarring; also called Oriental sore.">cutaneous leishmaniasis</term> (Oriental sore)

items: Occurs in the Old World: Africa, Asia, the Middle East.
Vector: Phlebotomus sandfly.
Reservoirs: dogs, foxes and rodents.
Other species causing cutaneous disease: L. aethiopica, L. major, L. infantum.
L. mexicana causes cutaneous disease in the New World (bay sore, chiclero ulcerMucocutaneous leishmaniasis, named after workers on chicle sap farms.).

blocks.x: Clinical picture: incubation 2–8 weeks. A red papule appears at the bite, becomes itchy, enlarges and ulcerates. The ulcer becomes hard and crusted and exudes serous material. Lesions may heal in a few months but leave disfiguring scars.
Leishmania braziliensis — <term d="Leishmaniasis spreading to the mucous membranes of nose, pharynx, palate and lips.">mucocutaneous leishmaniasis</term>

items: Occurs in the New World (Central and South America).
Vector: Lutzomyia sandfly. Reservoir: dogs.
Common among workers on chicle sap farms (the sap used to make chewing gum) — hence "chiclero ulcer".

blocks.x: Clinical picture: incubation 2–8 weeks for papules. Promastigotes then spread via the lymphatics to the nose, pharynx, palate and lips, destroying mucous membranes and the tissues around them. Invasion of the pharynx may cause loss of speech. The result is severe disfigurement and facial mutilation.

Leishmania donovani — <term d="Leishmaniasis of the internal organs, also called kala-azar.">visceral leishmaniasis</term> (<term d="Visceral leishmaniasis; the name means 'black fever', from the darkening of the skin.">kala-azar</term>)

items: Attacks the internal organs: liver, spleen, lungs, intestine.
Occurs in Africa, Asia, South and Central America.
Vector: Phlebotomus sandfly. Reservoirs: dogs, foxes, porcupines.

blocks.x: Clinical picture: incubation several weeks to 1 year. Begins with fever, diarrhoea and anaemia, then intermittent chills and sweating that can mimic malaria. As parasites invade liver and spleen these organs enlarge. There is weight loss and emaciation. Advanced disease brings kidney damage and granulomatous skin lesions, and the skin may darken — which is what "kala-azar" means: black fever. Untreated chronic cases usually die within 1–2 years.

sections.title: Finding the parasite, and killing it

blocks.x: Microscopy — the gold standard

items: Demonstrating amastigotes in blood smears and tissue aspirates (bone marrow, spleen, lymph nodes) is the gold standard.
For cutaneous disease, take smears from an ulcer biopsy.
Fixed smears are stained with Giemsa and examined under oil immersion.
Promastigotes may be seen in blood, bone marrow and tissue culture.

blocks.x: Other methods

items: Culture in NNN medium (Novy–MacNeal–Nicolle), or animal inoculation.
Molecular: PCR on clinical specimens.
Skin test: the Leishmanin (Montenegro) test.
Serology: ELISA, detecting either antibodies to the parasite or parasite antigen.

blocks.x: Treatment

items: Mucocutaneous disease responds poorly — treatment is usually ineffective.
Secondary bacterial infections are treated with antibiotics.
Visceral leishmaniasis: pentavalent antimonials given IV or IM are the drugs of choice — sodium stibogluconate (20 mg/kg daily for 28 days) and meglumine antimoniate.
Alternatives: amphotericin B, paromomycin, miltefosine.

blocks.x: Prevention and control

items: Protection from bites: screening, protective clothing, repellents, insecticide-impregnated bednets, and netting on windows and doors.
Treat all infected people promptly and eradicate ulcers to cut transmission — the human is a source as well as a victim.

blocks.x: A change of animal here: the sandfly is an insect, but the scabies mite is an arachnid. It is a permanent ectoparasite that lives in the skin rather than on it, and it is found worldwide.

items: Organism: Sarcoptes scabiei
Habitat: permanent ectoparasite in subcutaneous tissues (the burrow lies in the epidermis)
Distribution: worldwide
Diseases: scabies, also called acariasis or Norwegian itch

blocks.x: Class Arachnida — how a mite differs from an insect
Every one of these is a possible one-mark question, and all of them are "what an insect has, an arachnid does not":

items: Head and thorax are fused into the prosoma; the abdomen is the opisthosoma; when abdomen and prosoma fuse, the whole body is the idiosoma.
No wings.
No antennae and no compound eyes.
Four pairs of legs (insects have three).
A false head, the capitulum, at the front of the idiosoma.

blocks.x: Mouthparts

items: Pedipalps — sensory palps.
Chelicerae — for piercing and cutting.
Lips — the epistome and hypostome.
Absent: no maxillae, no mandibles, no hypopharynx.

sections.title: What the adult mite looks like

items: Size: 0.3–0.5 mm — scarcely visible to the naked eye.
Shape and colour: whitish, oval or disc-shaped, flattened ventrally and convex dorsally.
Dorsal cuticle: soft and striated with wavy parallel lines.
Dorsal spines: peg-like protuberances that point backwards all over the body — these act like a ratchet, helping the mite drive forwards through skin but not slip back.
No eyes, no tracheae.
No distinct head; palps short and fat; pincer-like chelicerae; hypostome untoothed.

blocks.x: The legs — and how to sex a mite

items: Four pairs of brown, stumpy legs, each divided into five ring-like segments.
The anterior two pairs are well separated from the posterior pairs.
Female: the first two pairs end in a stalk (pedicel) bearing suckers; the 3rd and 4th pairs end in long conspicuous bristles.
Male: the 4th (posterior) pair ends in suckers.

blocks.x: The rule to memorise: suckers on the 4th pair means male; bristles on the 3rd and 4th pairs means female.
An obligatory parasite that thrives and multiplies only on human skin. The female's tunnel is the whole story of the disease.
The burrow

items: Females excavate thin, tortuous tunnels in the epidermis, specifically the stratum corneum.
They choose skin that is delicate, thin and wrinkled: hands, wrists, groin, elbows, external genitalia, breast nipples, buttocks.
In children the mite may burrow into the face and feet.
It avoids the soles of the feet, palms of the hands, back and chest in adults.
Entry is achieved by the cutting edges of the tibiae of the front legs and the pincer-like chelicerae.
Disappearing into the skin takes about 2–20 minutes, depending on ambient temperature.
Once inside, the burrow lengthens by 2–3 mm per day, assisted by the hind legs and the backward-pointing dorsal spines.
Tunnels run more or less parallel to the surface.
The female feeds on liquid oozing from destroyed cells and is normally found at the blind end of the tunnel — which is exactly where to scrape for diagnosis.
Inside the tunnel, eggs and faecal spots alternate.

blocks.x: From egg to adult

items: Oval eggs are laid at 2–3 per day; the female lives about 1–2 months.
Eggs hatch in 3–5 days into a six-legged larva (hexapod) that resembles the adult.
Larvae excavate a pocket off the parent's burrow, or in a hair follicle.
After 2–3 days the larva moults into an eight-legged nymph (octopod).
A second moult produces either an adult male, or a sexually immature female / a second nymph that becomes the adult female.
Mating: males wander over the skin searching for burrows containing females. Copulation occurs only between an adult male and an adult female, and the male dies after copulation.
Egg to egg: 14–31 days.

blocks.x: Six legs then eight is the detail most often tested: the larva is the only six-legged stage.
Scabies is a contagious complaint spread by direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact.
Who does the spreading

items: The gravid female
The fertilized female
Active immature stages

blocks.x: Risk factors

items: Intrafamilial contact — including roommates
Overcrowding and lack of water supply
Sexual promiscuity
A seasonal trend in temperate zones
Affects all social classes ("scabies in the elite"), both sexes and all ages
Can be acquired from domestic animals (mange)

blocks.x: Higher-risk groups: sexually active adults, prison inmates, people in institutional care, people living in crowded conditions, and people in child care facilities.
Where the mites live on the body

items: Between the fingers; folds of the wrist, elbow or knee
Around the waistline and navel
On the breasts or genitals
In very young children: the head, neck, face, palms and soles

blocks.x: Site frequency — adults versus children
The contrast is the point: adults are bitten on the hands, children on the feet.
The mite itself is almost invisible; the disease you see is an allergic reaction to it. That single idea explains the rash, the timing, and why the itch outlasts the cure.

items: Produces a follicular papular rash, and the rash is visible even though the mite is not.
Characterised by excruciating pruritus (itching), intense at night.
The itch is caused by toxic secretions and faecal particles deposited in the burrow.
The disease has decreased with civilisation and cleanliness.

blocks.x: Complications

items: Frequently leads to secondary bacterial infection — especially impetigo.
Also eczema, boils and pustules; the skin weeps and bleeds.

blocks.x: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies

A very severe infestation involving tens of thousands of mites on one person, producing thick crusts full of mites and eggs. It occurs mainly in people with weakened immune systems, the elderly, and people who are disabled. It is highly contagious and needs swift treatment. The logic is worth noting: a weaker immune response means less itching, so less scratching, so the mites multiply unchecked.
Diagnosis

Usually clinical — a doctor identifies scabies from the appearance of the rash and the patient's description of the itch. A skin scraping may confirm it: skin from the affected area is examined under a microscope for mites, eggs or faecal matter.
Treatment

items: Benzyl benzoate (emulsion)
Sulphur ointment / Tetmosol
Mitigal cream or paint
Permethrin cream
Lindane — an organochlorine scabicide
Oral ivermectin
Treat all secondary bacterial infections

blocks.x: Itch relief

Scabicides kill mites and eggs but give no immediate itch relief. Antihistamine tablets help, especially at night. Hydrocortisone cream may help too, but it changes the appearance of the rash and makes diagnosis harder — so use it only after the diagnosis is confirmed.
Who needs treating

Everyone in close physical contact — bathing together, sharing a bed, even holding hands. Doctors usually treat all household members even without symptoms, because symptoms can take four to six weeks to appear. In daycare centres, classmates and caregivers usually need treatment too, since young children play with constant skin contact and share mats and blankets.
Ridding the home

Mites survive two to three days off the host on clothes, bedding or towels. Wash anything used in the past three days in hot water and dry in a hot dryer, or dry-clean it. Items that cannot be washed go in a sealed plastic bag for seven days.
Cautions

items: Treat all family members — it is contagious.
Boil clothes; abandon them if necessary.
Avoid public toilets and soiled linen.
Fumigate homes, hospitals and schools.

blocks.x: How soon does it go away?

Medication kills mites and eggs quickly and patients can usually return to school or work 24 hours after starting treatment. The itch may persist for a few weeks because of the ongoing allergic reaction — that is expected, not treatment failure. If itching lasts more than four weeks, or a new rash appears, the medication may need reapplying.
